stem: According to 'Dental Ethics and Law', what is described as the common strand linking ethics and law in professional practice?
options: Both provide the standard expected by society, identified by ethics and upheld by law
Both are enforced solely through financial penalties
Ethics is legally binding while law is optional guidance
Law defines morality and ethics has no independent role
justification: The Preface states that ethics and law share 'the common strand...that it provides the standard expected by society, identified by the former and upheld by the latter', meaning ethics identifies the standard and law upholds it.

stem: How is professional self-regulation of dentistry by the General Dental Council (GDC) characterised in the opening chapter?
options: A bargain or contract between the profession and the state for maintaining the highest standards of care
A purely administrative licensing function with no accountability
An arrangement funded entirely by government taxation
A voluntary scheme dentists may opt out of at will
justification: The chapter states it 'is often stated that professional self-regulation is a bargain or a contract between the profession and the state for the maintenance of the highest standards of care and for the protection of the public'.

stem: Under the Dentists Act described in the text, what special provision exists for a dentist over the age of 65 regarding registration fees?
options: They can apply for the 'retired practitioner's rate'
They are automatically exempt from all fees
They must pay double the retention fee
They are removed from the register without option to remain
justification: The text notes there is no reduced rate for part-time practitioners, 'but a practitioner over 65 can apply for the 'retired practitioner's rate''.

stem: What is the title of the GDC's ethical guidance document, first published in November 1997, that focuses on best practice for dentists?
options: Maintaining Standards
The First Five Years
Dental Practice Handbook
Code of Professional Conduct
justification: The chunk states 'The ethical guidance entitled Maintaining Standards, first published in November 1997, aims to be positive and focuses on best practice rather than conduct which can lead to disciplinary action'.

stem: According to the principles of justice discussed in the ethics chapters, on what basis should healthcare resources be fairly distributed?
options: Based on need rather than income or status
Based strictly on ability to pay privately
Based on the patient's occupation and social class
Based on order of registration with the practice
justification: The text states 'Justice also calls for resources to be fairly distributed, based on need rather than income or status', citing that elderly, sick or disabled patients have as much right to care as young, healthy patients.

stem: What term did 19th-century practitioners of dentistry in Europe use to describe themselves, before formal scientific training was established?
options: Surgeon-dentists
Registered dental officers
Licensed practitioners
Oral physicians
justification: The history section states 'those who practised dentistry in the 19th century were called 'surgeon-dentists'. They lacked any scientific knowledge and often inflicted harm on their patients'.

stem: Under paragraph 4.2 of Maintaining Standards, what is stated about a dentist who is aware of being infected with a bloodborne virus and takes no action?
options: The dentist is behaving unethically
The dentist must immediately stop all clinical work by law
The dentist is only at fault if a patient is actually infected
The dentist should self-report only if symptomatic
justification: The quoted guidance states 'A dentist who is aware of being infected with a bloodborne virus or any other transmissible disease or infection which might jeopardise the well-being of patients, and who takes no action, is behaving unethically'.

stem: In the chapter on resource allocation and business ethics, what ethical issues does the rationing of limited dental resources particularly raise?
options: Issues of justice and rights, particularly the right to health
Issues of taxation policy exclusively
Issues of dental material sourcing only
Issues unrelated to ethics, purely economic matters
justification: The chapter states 'Rationing is an ethical issue; in particular, it raises issues of justice and rights (particularly the right to health)'.

stem: When a dentist faces competing new materials and techniques each claiming superiority, what ethical dilemma does the text highlight regarding treatment recommendations?
options: Whether they should recommend less than the best, the best, or the optimum treatment
Whether patients should be charged extra for consultations
Whether advertising claims must be independently verified by law
Whether dental materials require government stockpiling
justification: The text asks whether practitioners facing competing claims of effectiveness 'should recommend less than the best, the best or the optimum', framing this as a constant source of ethical soul searching.

stem: Kant's categorical imperative, discussed in the chapter on the clinical relationship, demands that we treat humanity in ourselves or others in what way?
options: Never simply as a means but always at the same time as an end
Only as a means to achieving efficient clinical outcomes
As subordinate to the dentist's professional judgement
As a legal formality rather than a moral consideration
justification: The text cites Kant's categorical imperative that demands we treat 'humanity in your own person or in the person of any other never simply as a means but always at the same time as an end'.

stem: In the conclusion on the clinical relationship, what precondition does the interactive model of dentist-patient dialogue require of the dentist?
options: That the dentist is an effective communicator
That the dentist has completed a law degree
That the dentist only treats adult patients
That the dentist works exclusively within the NHS
justification: The text explains that determining what an individual patient wants 'may only be determined by the employment of an interactive model for the relationship, with the precondition that the dentist is an effective communicator'.

stem: If a patient's spouse rings the surgery asking whether her husband is having dental treatment there, what does the confidentiality chapter suggest the dentist should consider?
options: Whether the information is confidential and how the dentist would feel if their own information were shared
That all family members automatically have a right to this information
That the receptionist may freely disclose treatment details to any caller
That confidentiality only applies to written records, not phone calls
justification: The chunk poses the scenario of a wife who 'rings to ask if her husband is having dental treatment' and suggests considering the situation 'from the patient's position... how we would feel about our own information being known to others'.

stem: What right did the Data Protection Act 1998 extend to patients regarding the processing of their personal information?
options: Control to prevent information being used without their consent and the right to be informed by any data controller
The right to demand free duplicate copies of all radiographs
The right to have all records destroyed after one year
The right to appoint a family member as sole record custodian
justification: The text states the Act 'extends their control to prevent information obtained, by any healthcare professional, being used without their consent and requires that they are 'to be informed by any data controller''.

stem: According to the GDC's ethical guidance quoted in the consent chapter, how should a dentist act as a member of a caring profession?
options: In the best interests of the patient
In the best financial interests of the practice
According to the preferences of the referring specialist
In accordance with insurance company recommendations
justification: The chunk quotes the GDC guidance which 'exhorts that 'as a member of a caring profession...a dentist will act in the best interests of the patient'', reflecting the principle of beneficence.

stem: What legal consequence follows if a dentist performs an operation without a patient's consent, according to Justice Cardozo's statement cited in the consent chapter?
options: The surgeon commits an assault (battery) for which they are liable in damages
The surgeon is automatically referred to the GDC with no civil liability
The patient forfeits any right to complain if treatment succeeds
The dentist is only liable if the treatment caused physical harm
justification: Justice Cardozo's statement is quoted: 'a surgeon who performs an operation without his patient's consent commits an assault [sic. battery] for which he is liable in damages'.

stem: Under the Children Act 1989 as described in the text, what concept now governs who can consent to dental treatment on behalf of a child?
options: Parental responsibility
Legal guardianship registration only
Automatic maternal consent rights
School authority consent
justification: The text explains that rights and duties previously accorded to a parent, including the right to consent to medical treatment, 'are now replaced by the concept of 'parental responsibility'' under the Children Act 1989.

stem: Andrew Bridgman's chapter on informed consent opens with a quotation stating that, at its core, informed consent is what?
options: Respect for the patient as an individual, not a defense against a later malpractice suit
A legal formality required only for surgical procedures
A financial safeguard for the dental practice
A bureaucratic requirement imposed by insurers
justification: The chapter opens with the quotation: 'At its core, it is respect for the patient as an individual, not as a defense against the possibility of later malpractice suit' (Jory Graham).

stem: As a moral concept rather than a mere legal endpoint, how is informed consent described in the text?
options: As a process involving a two-way exchange of information between dentist and patient
As a single signature obtained before treatment begins
As an optional courtesy with no bearing on treatment validity
As a formality completed exclusively by administrative staff
justification: The text contrasts the legal view with the moral concept: 'the doctrine is more of a process in which there is a two-way exchange of information in order to help the dentist understand the patient's needs and expectations'.

stem: When parents speak little English and dental treatment is complex, such as long-term management of a child with a cleft palate, what does the text say is essential before treatment begins?
options: A bilingual health advocate
A signed waiver from the local school
Referral to a different practice entirely
A delay of treatment until the child learns English
justification: The text states that for complex cases such as 'the long-term management of treatment for a child with a cleft palate...a bilingual health advocate is essential before embarking on treatment'.

stem: In assessing decision-making capacity of patients with mental disability, what does the text say a dentist should do with the views of family and carers?
options: Take them into account but do so with caution
Disregard them entirely as legally irrelevant
Treat them as automatically overriding the patient's own wishes
Only accept them if provided in writing by a solicitor
justification: The text concludes that 'a dentist needs to take into account the views of others but should do so with caution', after outlining a range of attitudes toward patients' decision-making capacity.

stem: The chapter on practising in the NHS opens with a quotation from Aneurin Bevan about what condition disqualifying a society from calling itself civilised?
options: Denying medical aid to a sick person because of lack of means
Failing to provide free dental check-ups annually
Allowing private dental practices to operate
Restricting access to specialist orthodontic care
justification: The chapter epigraph reads: 'No society can legitimately call itself civilised if a sick person is denied medical aid because of lack of means...' (Aneurin Bevan, 1941).

stem: According to the NHS records section, for how long must a dentist retain a patient's records after completion of a course of treatment?
options: Two years
Six months
Ten years
Indefinitely with no minimum specified
justification: The chapter states the keeping of satisfactory records is of paramount importance and well-documented records form the basis of the defence to allegations; it specifies 'there is a requirement to retain the records for two years after completion of a course of treatment (paragraph 25(2))'.

stem: In negligence and litigation, what is generally said to be the precursor to litigation when a patient is dissatisfied with treatment?
options: A complaint, which provides an opportunity for resolution
An immediate court summons
A referral to the Dental Reference Service only
A mandatory GDC hearing
justification: The chapter opens by stating 'it is often said that complaints are the precursors of litigation. A complaint, in whatever form it arises, provides an opportunity for resolution but if it is not resolved, the patient may resort to litigation'.

stem: In Scotland, what is the term for the award made to a patient to compensate for pain and suffering following a breach of a legal duty causing injury?
options: Solatium
Provisional damages
Legal privilege
Contribution principle
justification: The text explains 'the patient is made an award of solatium to compensate for their pain and suffering and patrimonial loss to compensate for their financial losses'.

stem: According to the Declaration of Helsinki as discussed in the research ethics chapter, what basic premise is maintained regarding a doctor's priorities?
options: The health of a patient is a doctor's first consideration
Research outcomes take precedence over individual patient welfare
Informed consent is optional if the research benefits society
A physician's institutional obligations outweigh patient interests
justification: The text states that under the Declaration of Helsinki 'the basic premise is maintained that 'the health of a patient is a doctor's first consideration'', incorporated into the International Code of Medical Ethics.

stem: According to the chapter on professional duties, why is good communication among members of the dental team, including hygienist, nurse, receptionist and technician, important?
options: It avoids misunderstandings in the dental team and adds to the efficiency of a practice
It is required only for legal record-keeping purposes
It replaces the need for written treatment notes
It is relevant only to communication with patients, not team members
justification: The text states 'Good communication avoids misunderstandings in the dental team and adds to the efficiency of a practice', extending this to the hygienist, dental nurse, receptionist, dental technician and practice manager.
